claim: Alpha oscillations at about 10 Hz are often thought to arise from synchronous activity across the occipital cortex and are usually largest when the cortex is inactive.
source: Neuronal oscillations at about 10 Hz, called alpha oscillations, are often thought to arise from synchronous activity across the occipital cortex and are usually largest when the cortex is inactive.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing established understanding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Recent studies measuring visual receptive fields have reported that local alpha power increases when cortex is excited by visual stimulation.
source: However, recent studies measuring visual receptive fields have reported that local alpha power increases when cortex is excited by visual stimulation.
evidence: This statement references recent findings from other studies, as cited in the introduction.

claim: Stimulus-driven local increases in alpha power result from a mixture of two effects: a reduction in alpha oscillatory power and a simultaneous increase in broadband power.
source: We hypothesized that stimulus-driven local increases in alpha power result from a mixture of two effects: a reduction in alpha oscillatory power and a simultaneous increase in broadband power.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study, tested through modeling and data analysis.

claim: Alpha pRFs have similar center locations to pRFs estimated from broadband power but are several times larger.
source: We find that the alpha pRFs have similar center locations to pRFs estimated from broadband power but are several times larger
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Alpha oscillatory power decreases in response to stimuli within the receptive field.
source: alpha oscillatory power decreases in response to stimuli within the receptive field, reinforcing the link between alpha oscillations and cortical inactivity
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through the spectral decomposition method and pRF modeling shown in Figures 2, 3, and 7.

claim: Broadband power increases in response to visual stimulation.
source: whereas broadband power increases
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral density analyses in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Hans Berger first measured electrical oscillations at 10 Hz from the human brain using EEG.
source: Hans Berger first measured electrical oscillations at 10 Hz from the human brain using EEG (Berger, 1929).
evidence: This is a historical fact cited from Berger's 1929 work.

claim: When a participant closes their eyes or views a uniform field, alpha oscillatory power increases.
source: Shortly thereafter, Adrian and Matthews, 1934 confirmed that when a participant closes their eyes or views a uniform field, the oscillatory power increases.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited from Adrian and Matthews 1934.

claim: Alpha oscillatory power is reduced by arousal and alertness.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, alpha oscillatory power is reduced by arousal (Barry et al., 2007) and alertness (Matousek and Petersén, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2007 and Matousek and Petersén, 1983.

claim: When attending a location to the left or right of fixation, occipital alpha power measured by EEG decreases contralaterally and increases ipsilaterally.
source: For example, when attending a location to the left or right of fixation, the occipital alpha power measured by EEG decreases contralaterally and increases ipsilaterally (Kelly et al., 2006; Sauseng et al., 2005; Worden et al., 2000), opposite to the fMRI response (reviewed by Carrasco, 2011; Somers et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to EEG studies.

claim: The reduction in alpha power can be specific to cortical locations representing narrow angular wedges in the visual field, as measured by both EEG and MEG.
source: The reduction in alpha power can also be specific to cortical locations representing narrow angular wedges in the visual field, as measured by both EEG and MEG (Foster et al., 2017; Popov et al., 2019; Rihs et al., 2007; Samaha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple EEG and MEG studies.

claim: Two studies in macaque measured spatial receptive fields using power in the alpha band and found that for most recording sites, alpha power increased rather than decreased when a stimulus was in the receptive field.
source: Specifically, two studies in macaque measured spatial receptive fields using power in the alpha band as a dependent measure, and found that for most recording sites, alpha power increased rather than decreased when a stimulus was in the receptive field (Klink et al., 2021; Takaura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on citations to Klink et al., 2021 and Takaura et al., 2016.

claim: Human intracortical studies have reported power increases in the alpha band when stimuli were in or near electrode receptive fields.
source: A positive association has also been found in human intracortical studies, reporting power increases in the alpha band when stimuli were in or near electrode receptive fields (Harvey et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harvey et al., 2013 and Luo et al., 2024.

claim: Broadband spectral power increases are observed in many intracranial studies in association with increased neural activity.
source: Broadband spectral power increases are observed in many intracranial studies in association with increased neural activity (Crone et al., 1998; Hermes et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2009a; Winawer et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to intracranial studies.

claim: Broadband signals likely have a distinct biological cause from oscillations.
source: and likely have a distinct biological cause from oscillations (Hermes et al., 2017; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hermes et al., 2017 and Ray and Maunsell, 2011.

claim: Broadband power changes can extend to low frequencies, including the alpha band.
source: because broadband power changes can extend to low frequencies, including the alpha band (Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winawer et al., 2013.

claim: ECoG data were recorded from 9 participants implanted with subdural electrodes for clinical purposes.
source: ECoG data were recorded from 9 participants implanted with subdural electrodes for clinical purposes.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Data from seven patients were collected at New York University Grossman School of Medicine (NYU), and from two patients at the University Medical Center Utrecht (UMCU).
source: Data from seven patients were collected at New York University Grossman School of Medicine (NYU), and from two patients at the University Medical Center Utrecht (UMCU).
evidence: This describes the data collection sites.

claim: Visual stimulation causes a broadband increase in power spanning frequencies from 1 to 150 Hz.
source: The stimulus causes a broadband power increase, spanning frequencies from 1 to 150 Hz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1e and described in the text.

claim: During blank trials, there is a peak in the spectrum at around 13 Hz (alpha oscillation).
source: During the blank, but not during visual stimulation, there is a peak in the spectrum at around 13 Hz (alpha oscillation, dashed vertical line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The broadband and alpha response amplitudes and estimated pRF locations are little affected by ERP regression.
source: The broadband and alpha response amplitudes, along with the estimated pRF locations, are shown for three representative electrodes depicted in Figure 1 and Figure 2. These summary metrics are little affected by ERP regression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The cross-validated variance explained in the pRF models is nearly identical for broadband with vs without ERP regression.
source: Except for a handful of electrodes in Dorsolateral maps, the cross-validated variance explained in the pRF models is nearly identical for broadband with vs without ERP regression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The power at the peak alpha frequency for stimulus relative to blank increased slightly for electrode Oc18, decreased slightly for electrode Oc17, and decreased more substantially for electrode Oc25.
source: Due to the interaction with the broadband response, the power at the peak alpha frequency for stimulus relative to blank increased slightly for one electrode (Oc18), decreased slightly for a second electrode (Oc17), and decreased more substantially for a third electrode (Oc25).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and described in the text.

claim: After correcting for the broadband shift, the alpha oscillation is suppressed by visual stimulation for all three electrodes (Oc17, Oc18, Oc25).
source: By adjusting the baseline to account for the broadband response as shown in the right panels, it is clear that the stimulus caused the alpha oscillation to decrease for all three electrodes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 right panels.

claim: The pRF model accurately predicted the broadband and alpha time series for electrode GB103, with twofold cross-validated variance explained of 90.2% for broadband and 69.5% for alpha.
source: The pRF models accurately predicted these time series, with twofold cross-validated variance explained of 90.2% for broadband and 69.5% for alpha.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and described in the text.

claim: For electrode GB103, the alpha pRF is about twice the size of the broadband pRF.
source: For both types of pRF, the center locations are in the parafovea in the left lower visual field, but the alpha pRF is about twice the size of the broadband pRF (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: For visually selective electrodes in V1 to V3, the alpha pRF model explains 37% of the cross-validated variance in the alpha time series.
source: We find that for visually selective electrodes in V1 to V3, the alpha pRF model explains 37% of the cross-validated variance in the alpha time series (Figure 4, 'All Patients').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and described in the text.

claim: For non-visually selective electrodes, the pRF model explains close to 0% of the variance.
source: The non-visually selective electrodes provide a null distribution for comparison, and for these electrodes, the pRF model explains close to 0% of the variance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: In dorsolateral maps beyond V1–V3, the alpha pRF model explained about 24% of the variance in visually responsive electrodes.
source: In dorsolateral maps beyond V1–V3, the alpha pRF model explained about 24% of the variance in visually responsive electrodes, and no variance in the non-responsive group (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The polar angles are highly similar between broadband and alpha both in V1–V3 (r=0.98) and dorsolateral visual areas (r=0.95).
source: First, the polar angles are highly similar between broadband and alpha both in V1–V3 (r=0.98) and dorsolateral visual areas (r=0.95).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The eccentricities are correlated but not equal (r=0.68, 0.09): the alpha pRFs tend to have larger eccentricities than the broadband pRFs, especially in dorsolateral visual areas.
source: Second, the eccentricities are correlated but not equal (r=0.68, 0.09): the alpha pRFs tend to have larger eccentricities than the broadband pRFs, especially in dorsolateral visual areas.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The sizes of alpha pRFs correlate with those of broadband pRFs (r=0.33, 0.24), but are about 2–4 times larger.
source: Third, the sizes of alpha pRFs also correlate with those of broadband pRFs (r=0.33, 0.24), but are about 2–4 times larger.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: For both broadband pRFs and alpha pRFs, the pRF size systematically increases with eccentricity.
source: Contrary to this possibility, we find that for both broadband pRFs and alpha pRFs, the pRF size systematically increases with eccentricity (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), consistent with known properties of visual neurons (Newsome et al., 1986) and with fMRI data (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008; Kay et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1d, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The slopes of the size vs. eccentricity functions are about three times larger for alpha than for broadband (slopes: 0.53 vs 0.15 in V1–V3; 1.17 vs 0.40 in dorsolateral, for alpha vs broadband).
source: The slopes of the size vs. eccentricity functions are about three times larger for alpha than for broadband (slopes: 0.53 vs 0.15 in V1–V3; 1.17 vs 0.40 in dorsolateral, for alpha vs broadband).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The pRFs for the low frequency broadband response had a positive gain and a small size, similar to the high-frequency broadband response (sizes: 1.0 vs 1.1 vs 2.3 deg, for high-frequency broadband vs low-frequency broadband vs alpha).
source: Unlike the alpha pRFs, which had negative gain and a large size, the pRFs for the low frequency broadband response had a positive gain and a small size, similar to the high-frequency broadband response (sizes: 1.0 vs 1.1 vs 2.3 deg, for high-frequency broadband vs low-frequency broadband vs alpha; Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cross-validated variance explained was about 4 times higher when correcting for the baseline (43% vs 10%, median).
source: First, the cross-validated variance explained was about 4 times higher when correcting for the baseline (43% vs 10%, median).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: With baseline correction, pRF gain is consistently negative (29 out of 31 electrodes), meaning that alpha oscillations are suppressed by stimuli in the receptive field.
source: Second, as expected, the baseline-corrected approach consistently results in negative gain (29 out of 31 electrodes), meaning that alpha oscillations are suppressed by stimuli in the receptive field.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 middle panel.

claim: Without baseline correction, there is a mixture of positive and negative gain (14 negative, 17 positive).
source: In contrast, with no baseline correction, there is a mixture of positive and negative gain (14 negative, 17 positive), complicating the interpretation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 middle panel.

claim: With baseline correction, pRF size increases with eccentricity, but without baseline correction, it does not.
source: Third, with baseline correction, pRF size increases with eccentricity, but without baseline correction, it does not.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 right panel.

claim: Coherence declines with distance, with alpha coherence about 0.6 between neighboring electrodes, declining to a baseline level of about 0.35 by about 1 cm.
source: First, as expected, coherence declines with distance. The alpha coherence is about 0.6 between neighboring electrodes, declining to a baseline level of about 0.35 by about 1 cm.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: The coherence was higher at the alpha frequency than in the broadband frequencies, especially between neighboring electrodes.
source: Second, the coherence was higher at the alpha frequency than in the broadband frequencies, especially between neighboring electrodes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8.

claim: The highest coherence is at the peak alpha frequency.
source: The highest coherence is at the peak alpha frequency (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: A population of high threshold thalamocortical neurons generates bursts in the alpha or theta frequency range.
source: Recent work has identified a population of high threshold thalamocortical neurons that generates bursts in the alpha or theta frequency range (depending on membrane potential) (Hughes and Crunelli, 2007; Hughes et al., 2011; Lorincz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hughes and Crunelli, 2007; Hughes et al., 2011; Lorincz et al., 2009.

claim: These bursts are synchronized by gap junctions.
source: These bursts are synchronized by gap junctions.
evidence: This is stated in the context of discussing the biological origins of alpha oscillations, based on cited literature.

claim: Feedback signals from V1 to LGN via corticothalamic cells can modulate the frequency and amplitude of the alpha generating thalamocortical cells.
source: Feedback signals from V1 to LGN via corticothalamic cells can modulate the frequency and amplitude of the alpha generating thalamocortical cells (Hughes and Crunelli, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hughes and Crunelli, 2007.

claim: The broadband signal is not limited to a narrow frequency range.
source: First and most obvious, the signal is not limited to a narrow frequency range (Hermes et al., 2015; Hermes et al., 2017; Hermes et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2009a; Winawer et al., 2013), and hence is not generally considered an oscillation (Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Broadband signals are found throughout the brain.
source: Second, broadband signals are found throughout the brain (Kupers et al., 2018; Manning et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014), likely arising from non-oscillatory neural generators (Bédard et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2009a)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The alpha rhythm is largest in the occipital lobe.
source: whereas the alpha rhythm is largest in the occipital lobe.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience.

claim: The broadband signal measured at the electrode has lower amplitude because the generators are not synchronized across space.
source: Finally, the broadband signal measured at the electrode has lower amplitude because the generators are not synchronized across space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of broadband signal generation.

claim: Klink et al., 2021 fit pRF models to electrode data from macaque primary visual cortex in many frequency bands, including alpha, without removing the broadband signal, and found no systematic relationship between pRF size and eccentricity.
source: Klink et al., 2021 fit pRF models to electrode data from macaque primary visual cortex in many frequency bands, including alpha, without removing the broadband signal. They found no systematic relationship between pRF size and eccentricity and found that the gain was positive for some electrodes and negative for others.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Klink et al., 2021.

claim: Takaura et al., 2016 estimated receptive fields in macaque in several frequency bands, including alpha, and found that alpha power tended to increase by visual stimulation.
source: Second, Takaura et al., 2016 estimated receptive fields in macaque in several frequency bands, including alpha. They found that alpha power tended to increase by visual stimulation, in contrast to our results.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Takaura et al., 2016.

claim: Harvey et al., 2013 examined spatial selectivity of human ECoG responses in the alpha band and reported that alpha power increased in V1 electrodes when stimuli were outside the pRF.
source: Finally, Harvey et al., 2013 examined spatial selectivity of human ECoG responses in the alpha band. They fit pRF models to the broadband response and then measured alpha power for stimulus positions relative to the broadband pRFs. They reported that alpha power increased in V1 electrodes when stimuli were outside the pRF, and that there was no change in alpha power when the stimulus overlapped the broadband pRF.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Harvey et al., 2013.

claim: In V1–V3, the stimulus-related broadband elevation is clear all the way down to 3 Hz or lower, whereas in dorsolateral cortex it is clear only down to about 25 Hz.
source: In V1–V3, the stimulus-related broadband elevation is clear all the way down to 3 Hz or lower, whereas in dorsolateral cortex it is clear only down to about 25 Hz.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The human microelectrode recordings indicate that broadband power extending as low as 2 Hz can be measured across many brain regions, including frontal, parietal, and occipital cortices as well as hippocampus and amygdala.
source: The human microelectrode recordings (Manning et al., 2009) indicate that broadband power extending as low as 2 Hz can be measured across many brain regions, including frontal, parietal, and occipital cortices as well as hippocampus and amygdala.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manning et al., 2009.

claim: The large size and the negative valence of alpha pRFs can explain key features of exogenous visual attention.
source: Finally, we show how the large size and the negative valence of alpha pRFs can explain key features of exogenous visual attention.
evidence: This is a claim made in the abstract and elaborated in the Discussion section.

claim: The spatial profiles of attention, measured behaviorally, and of the alpha pRF are quite similar, with three close parallels: the spatial spread increases with eccentricity, is asymmetric spreading further into the periphery than toward the fovea, and shows center/surround organization.
source: The relationship may be more than conceptual, however, as we find that the spatial profiles of attention, measured behaviorally (Downing and Pinker, 1985; Shulman et al., 1986), and of the alpha pRF are quite similar (Figure 10), with three close parallels. For both measures, the spatial spread (1) increases with eccentricity, (2) is asymmetric, spreading further into the periphery than toward the fovea, and (3) shows center/surround organization, with the attentional effect changing from a benefit to a cost and the alpha response changing from suppression to enhancement.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10 and supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Exogenous attention has a maximal effect at about 100ms, the duration of an alpha cycle.
source: The timing also matches, since exogenous attention has a maximal effect at about 100ms (Nakayama and Mackeben, 1989; Wang et al., 2015a), the duration of an alpha cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakayama and Mackeben, 1989 and Wang et al., 2015a.

claim: The stimulus causes a change in the alpha oscillation and this in turn causes increased neural responsivity and behavioral sensitivity, the hallmarks of covert spatial attention.
source: We propose that the stimulus causes a change in the alpha oscillation and this in turn causes increased neural responsivity and behavioral sensitivity, the hallmarks of covert spatial attention.
evidence: This is a proposal made by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Alpha oscillation is likely to play a role in how cortex encodes sensory information.
source: More generally, alpha oscillation is likely to play a role in how cortex encodes sensory information.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Fifty-three electrodes met the criteria for comparison between alpha and broadband pRFs, of which 35 are assigned to V1–V3 and 45 to dorsolateral maps.
source: This procedure resulted in 54 electrodes from four patients. Of these, 35 electrodes had non-zero probability assignments to V1, V2, or V3, 45 to dorsolateral visual areas (TO, LO, V3AB, or IPS), and three to ventral visual areas (hV4, VO, or PHC).
evidence: This describes the electrode selection for the comparison analysis.

claim: The percentage of the broadband pRF inside the alpha pRF was 92.3% (V1–V3) and 98.0% (dorsolateral) pRFs.
source: Truncating the pRF sizes at 1 standard deviation, the percentage of the broadband pRF inside the alpha pRF was 92.3% (V1–V3) and 98.0% (dorsolateral) pRFs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the pRF comparison analysis.

claim: If we shuffle the relationship between alpha and broadband pRFs across electrodes, the overlap decreases sharply, to 30.0% (V1–V3) and 25.7% (dorsolateral).
source: If we shuffle the relationship between alpha and broadband pRFs across electrodes, the overlap decreases sharply, to 30.0% (V1–V3) and 25.7% (dorsolateral).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis to test the significance of the overlap.

claim: The alpha pRF is negative, and alpha tends to be inhibitory, meaning that visual stimuli within the alpha pRF disinhibit cortex, the opposite of surround suppression.
source: First, the alpha pRF is negative, and alpha tends to be inhibitory (Bastos et al., 2020; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2010; Van Diepen et al., 2019), meaning that visual stimuli within the alpha pRF disinhibit cortex, the opposite of surround suppression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Surround suppression is relatively fast, disappearing 60ms after surround stimulus offset.
source: Surround suppression is relatively fast, disappearing 60ms after surround stimulus offset (Bair et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bair et al., 2003.

claim: Surround suppression is feature-specific.
source: Furthermore, surround suppression is feature-specific (Bair et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bair et al., 2003.

claim: The alpha oscillation, being coherent over several mm of cortex, is unlikely to be limited only to cells whose tuning match the stimulus.
source: whereas the alpha oscillation, being coherent over several mm of cortex, is unlikely to be limited only to cells whose tuning match the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coherence analysis results.

claim: Surround suppression may be linked to neural oscillations, albeit at a higher frequency range.
source: Nonetheless, surround suppression may be linked to neural oscillations, albeit at a higher frequency range (Hermes et al., 2019; Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hermes et al., 2019 and Ray et al., 2013.

claim: Oscillations decrease with saccade initiation.
source: Supporting evidence includes the observations that oscillations decrease with saccade initiation (Popov et al., 2021b)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Popov et al., 2021b.

claim: Saccades can be phase-locked to the alpha rhythm.
source: and that saccades can be phase-locked to the alpha rhythm (Drewes and VanRullen, 2011; Staudigl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drewes and VanRullen, 2011 and Staudigl et al., 2017.

claim: Simulations of pRFs in which the ground truth is known show no systematic increase in pRF size with more noise.
source: First, simulations of pRFs in which the ground truth is known show no systematic increase in pRF size with more noise (Lerma-Usabiaga et al., 2020, their Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lerma-Usabiaga et al., 2020.

claim: Adding substantial noise to real fMRI data had little to no effect on pRF size.
source: Second, adding substantial noise to real fMRI data had little to no effect on pRF size (Le et al., 2017, their Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Le et al., 2017.

claim: The larger size of the alpha pRFs is preserved when regressing size vs variance explained.
source: Third, the larger size of the alpha pRFs is preserved when regressing size vs variance explained (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are many parallels, and likely shared circuitry, between spatial attention and eye movements.
source: Nonetheless, there are many parallels, and likely shared circuitry, between spatial attention and eye movements (Moore and Fallah, 2001; Shepherd et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore and Fallah, 2001 and Shepherd et al., 1986.

claim: Oscillations in the alpha and beta range play a role in feedback between visual areas, with evidence from nonhuman primates for specificity of alpha and beta oscillations in cortical depth.
source: One claim is that oscillations in the alpha and beta range play a role in feedback between visual areas, with evidence from nonhuman primates for specificity of alpha and beta oscillations in cortical depth (Bastos et al., 2020; Bollimunta et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bastos et al., 2020 and Bollimunta et al., 2011.
